payload.name: resonant-peak
payload.scope: To quantify the maximum amplification in a closed-loop system's frequency response, so designers can assess relative stability and predict time-domain ringing.

definition.body: Resonant-peak is a human-made stability measure that quantifies the maximum magnitude of a closed-loop system's frequency response, occurring at the resonant frequency where the amplification is greatest. Parameters: (1) the closed-loop transfer function T(jw) = G(jw)/(1 + G(jw)H(jw)); (2) the resonant frequency wr where the magnitude of T(jw) achieves its maximum; (3) the peak magnitude Mr = max of the magnitude of T(jw) over all frequencies. For a standard second-order underdamped system, Mr = 1/(2*zeta*sqrt(1-zeta^2)) and wr = wn*sqrt(1-2*zeta^2), where zeta is the damping ratio, providing a direct quantitative link between frequency-domain amplification and time-domain transient quality. It is distinct from bandwidth (the frequency span where the gain exceeds -3 dB, not the maximum gain), gain-margin (the gain headroom at the -180 degree phase crossing, a different stability measure), and peak-overshoot (the time-domain exceedance of the steady-state value, not the frequency-domain amplification). Persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard relative-stability specification in classical control engineering - measured from the Bode magnitude curve of closed-loop frequency responses, computed from analytical transfer functions, and specified in design requirements for servo systems, filter design, and vibration control - encoded in control textbooks (Ogata's Modern Control Engineering; Franklin, Powell, and Workman's Digital Control of Dynamic Systems), simulation tools, and aerospace control design practice. e.g.: the resonant peak Mr = 1.15 of a second-order system with zeta=0.5, attained at wr = 0.71wn; the closed-loop peak of a second-order low-pass filter with zeta=0.4 read from the Bode magnitude curve as Mr = 1.36; the design guideline bounding Mr below 1.5 to limit step overshoot, per Ogata's Modern Control Engineering | not: bandwidth (the passband width, not the peak gain); gain-margin (the gain headroom at the -180 degree phase crossing, not the peak magnitude); peak-overshoot (the time-domain exceedance, not the frequency-domain amplification) [formal: culminans amplificatio | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: controllability
payload.scope: To provide a formal criterion for whether a system's inputs can steer its internal state to any desired value, so engineers can verify that control design is structurally feasible before investing in gain tuning.

definition.body: Controllability is a human-made mathematical concept that maps the reachability property of a dynamical system's state space through its input channels. The construct determines whether, for a linear time-invariant system described by ẋ = Ax + Bu, there exists an input function u(t) over a finite time interval that can drive the state from any initial condition to any final state. The standard test constructs the controllability matrix with columns B, AB, A²B through Aⁿ⁻¹B and checks whether its rank equals n, the state dimension. If rank is less than n, the system has uncontrollable modes — state directions that no input can affect. The concept persists through control theory pedagogy (taught in every linear systems course), engineering design checklists (verifying controllability before designing state-feedback controllers), and software tools (MATLAB's ctrb and iscontrollable functions). It is distinct from observability (state reconstruction from outputs), stabilizability (uncontrollable modes are stable), and detectability (observability analogue for stabilization). e.g.: controllability check for a mass-spring system with single force input; full-rank controllability matrix of a 3-state aircraft longitudinal model; uncontrollable mode in parallel RLC circuit with voltage source across capacitor | not: observability (reconstructing state from outputs, not driving via inputs); stabilizability (allowing uncontrollable modes only if stable); reachability (stronger: attainable in exactly the specified time) [formal: controllabilitas | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: riccati-equation
payload.scope: To provide a nonlinear matrix equation whose solution yields optimal feedback gains for linear systems with quadratic cost, and whose stability characterizations underpin Lyapunov theory in control and estimation.

definition.body: The Riccati equation is a human-made nonlinear matrix equation of the form A^T P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^T P + Q = 0 (continuous-time algebraic Riccati equation, or CARE), where A is the state matrix, B is the input matrix, Q is a symmetric positive semi-definite state-weighting matrix, and R is a symmetric positive definite input-weighting matrix, and P is the unknown symmetric matrix to be solved for. A discrete-time variant exists: A^T P A - P - (A^T P B)(R + B^T P B)^{-1}(B^T P A) + Q = 0. Parameters: matrices A, B, Q, R defining the system and cost; the solution matrix P. The equation persists as a computational object in optimal control synthesis, filter design (Kalman filter gain computation), differential game theory, and robust control — encoded in numerical software (MATLAB's care/dare, SciPy's solve_continuous_are), control theory textbooks (Anderson & Moore, Lancaster & Rodman), and aerospace/robotics design tools. e.g.: MATLAB's care function computing P for a quadcopter LQR design with Q=diag(1,1,0.1,0.1) and R=0.01*I; the CARE solution for a satellite attitude control problem yielding optimal gains for reaction wheel actuation; SciPy's solve_continuous_are applied to a DC motor velocity regulator with state weights for position and speed | not: linear matrix equation (linear in the unknown, not nonlinear quadratic); Lyapunov equation (A^T P + P A = -Q is the special case with no B R^{-1} B^T P term, i.e. R^{-1}=0) [formal: aequatio Riccati | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lqg
payload.scope: To provide optimal state-feedback combined with optimal state estimation when only noisy outputs are available, separating the design into independent LQR and Kalman-filter components.

definition.body: LQG (Linear Quadratic Gaussian) is a human-made optimal control synthesis procedure that combines an LQR state-feedback controller with a Kalman filter state estimator, using the separation principle: the control gain and estimator gain are designed independently and then combined into an output-feedback controller. Parameters: the LQR cost matrices (Q, R), the Kalman noise covariances (process noise W, measurement noise V), system matrices (A, B, C), and the resulting gain matrices (K for feedback, L for estimation). The closed-loop output is u = -K x_hat where x_hat is the Kalman-filter estimate. LQG persists as the standard linear stochastic control design method -- encoded in control textbooks (Kailath; Anderson & Moore), MATLAB lqg function, and industrial applications in aerospace guidance, robotics, and process control where states are unmeasurable. e.g.: MATLAB lqg design for a satellite attitude controller with LQR gains and Kalman filter for star-tracker outputs; LQG control of a quadcopter with IMU measurements feeding a Kalman observer; LQG-based autopilot for a fixed-wing aircraft using GPS position and barometer altitude as noisy measurements | not: LQR (no noise estimation, uses full state feedback only); Kalman filter alone (estimation only, not combined with optimal control); MPC (finite-horizon constrained optimization, not infinite-horizon stochastic) [formal: regulatio quadratica linearis gaussiana | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]
